title: Grounding: return attention to the present
summary: When you feel overwhelmed, gently notice your surroundings and senses. A 5–4–3–2–1 exercise can help direct attention to what is here now. You can stop or adapt it if it feels uncomfortable.
source: WHO — Doing What Matters in Times of Stress

title: Notice a thought without obeying it
summary: Try naming a thought as a thought rather than a fact: “I'm noticing the thought that I will fail.” You do not need to force it away. Consider what is known, what is uncertain, and one kinder alternative.
source: WHO — Doing What Matters in Times of Stress

title: Thoughts, feelings and actions are connected
summary: A CBT-informed reflection can help you notice how a situation, interpretation, feeling and action influence one another. Ask: what is the evidence, is there another explanation, and what small helpful action is possible?

title: Give worries a small container
summary: If worries keep interrupting the day, some people find it useful to write them down and set aside a brief, planned time to review them. Separate what you can act on from what is outside your control.

title: Small actions during stressful times
summary: Stress can make everything feel urgent. Pause, notice what matters to you, and choose one manageable next action. Connecting with someone supportive and treating yourself with kindness can also help.
source: WHO — Doing What Matters in Times of Stress

title: Build a gentle wind-down routine
summary: A consistent, calming routine and reducing stimulating activities before bed may support sleep. If sleep problems persist or affect daily life, consider speaking with a qualified health professional.

title: You do not have to manage alone
summary: If difficult feelings are persistent, intensifying, or interfering with everyday life, consider talking with a trusted person, school counsellor, or qualified mental health professional. Asking for help is a practical step, not a failure.
